2:2.text: And Israel dwelt in the land of Egypt, in the country of Goshen; and they had possessions therein, and grew, and multiplied exceedingly.

provenance.other: “multiplied exceedingly” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Exodus 1:7, the verse usually remembered for this, reads 'increased abundantly, and multiplied, and waxed exceeding mighty' — a different phrase. 'Waxed great' occurs in five verses and carries no weight on its own.
provenance.significance: Genesis 47:27 is the last verse of the settlement in Goshen and the hinge of the Exodus story: a family becomes a nation in a land it was given rather than born to, and the multiplication is what makes the next book's oppression possible. Mosiah 2:2 uses the phrase of a people who have likewise been brought into a land not their own, in the paragraph that gathers them for the covenant sermon. The Book of Mormon runs Exodus typology continuously from 1 Nephi 2 onward, and this is the Goshen verse.

2:2.note: 'For they had multiplied exceedingly, and waxed great in the land.' A KJV singleton doing the same narrative work as its source — the census-defeating growth of a transplanted people. Recorded as an echo rather than an allusion because a two-word formula is thin, and because the second clause ('waxed great in the land') is not from Genesis 47:27 and matches no KJV verse.

2:4.text: And the children of Israel remembered not the LORD their God, who had delivered them out of the hands of all their enemies on every side:

provenance.other: “delivered them out of the hands of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The KJV's much commoner idiom is 'delivered them INTO the hands of' their enemies (Judges 2:14 and many others), which is the opposite transaction; the deliverance direction with this exact string is Judges 8:34's alone.
provenance.significance: This is the register's best kind of finding and it turns on a single word of the source: 'remembered NOT'. Judges 8:34 is the KJV's one sentence about being delivered out of enemy hands, and it is a sentence about ingratitude — Israel forgot the God who did it, as soon as Gideon was dead. Mosiah 2:4 is a people assembled specifically to 'give thanks to the Lord their God, who … had delivered them out of the hands of their enemies', immediately before their own leader dies. The Book of Mormon has taken the words of the KJV's classic failure of gratitude and used them for an act of gratitude, at the moment Judges says gratitude fails.

2:4.note: Nine words in sequence, including the whole clause 'the Lord their God, who had delivered them out of the hands of', from a KJV verse the machine ranked first in the chapter and ranked correctly. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations; filed as an allusion rather than a quotation because the Book of Mormon breaks the clause with 'who had brought them out of the land of Jerusalem' before completing it. The reversal of Judges's sense is the argument.

2:5.text: And when the cloud was taken up from the tabernacle, then after that the children of Israel journeyed: and in the place where the cloud abode, there the children of Israel pitched their tents.

provenance.route: Numbers 9:17 with Numbers 2:2 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “pitched their tents” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and that verse pitches them at the tabernacle where the cloud rested. The arrangement — by household, each family separate, facing the sanctuary — is Numbers 2:2's: 'Every man of the children of Israel shall pitch by his own standard, with the ensign of their father's house: far off about the tabernacle of the congregation shall they pitch.'
provenance.significance: Two verses of Numbers supply the phrase and the floor plan of Israel's wilderness camp, and Mosiah 2:5-6 rebuilds that camp around a temple instead of a tabernacle, with the tent doors turned toward it. What the Book of Mormon adds is the doors, which Numbers does not specify — and that detail turns a camp into a congregation, since a door facing the sanctuary is a position for hearing rather than for marching. The scene is the wilderness camp reassembled for a sermon.

2:5.note: 'They pitched their tents round about, every man according to his family … every family being separate, one from another' — and in the next verse, 'every man having his tent with the door thereof towards the temple'. The phrase is a KJV singleton and the arrangement is Numbers 2:2's, household by household about the sanctuary. Note that the Feast of Tabernacles reading (Leviticus 23:42) is the usual one offered for this scene and is not what the wording supports: Leviticus has booths, not tents, and no orientation.

2:7.text: And Ezra the scribe stood upon a pulpit of wood, which they had made for the purpose; and beside him stood Mattithiah, and Shema, and Anaiah, and Urijah, and Hilkiah, and Maaseiah, on his right hand; and on his left hand, Pedaiah, and Mishael, and Malchiah, and Hashum, and Hashbadana, Zechariah, and Meshullam.

provenance.other: “pulpit of wood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “made for the purpose” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — the same verse. The English Bible has one purpose-built raised platform from which a leader addresses an assembled nation, and it is Ezra's.
provenance.significance: Nehemiah 8 is the KJV's only account of the scene Mosiah 2 stages: a whole people gathered in one place at the sanctuary, a leader raised on a structure erected specially so that he can be seen and heard, a reading of the law before men, women and everyone who could understand, and a covenant renewal that runs on for chapters. Benjamin's tower is Ezra's pulpit, his 'those that were not under the sound of his voice' answers Nehemiah 8:2's 'all that could hear with understanding', and the multi-day festal assembly that follows in Mosiah 3-6 answers Nehemiah 8-10. 1 Nephi 1:19 already reached this chapter of Nehemiah for a different detail, so it is not a first contact — but this is where the whole scene is taken.

2:7.note: 'The multitude being so great, that king Benjamin could not teach them all within the walls of the temple; therefore, he caused a tower to be erected.' No wording is reproduced — the Book of Mormon says 'tower' where the KJV says 'pulpit of wood' — so this is filed as conceptual, and the case rests on the fact that the KJV builds such a structure exactly once, for exactly this purpose, in a chapter whose other elements Mosiah 2 also has. Nehemiah 8:5 supplies the corollary the Book of Mormon keeps: Ezra was 'above all the people', and that is why he opened the book where they could see.

2:9.text: And he read therein before the street that was before the water gate from the morning until midday, before the men and the women, and those that could understand; and the ears of all the people were attentive unto the book of the law.

provenance.other: “hear with understanding” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “were attentive” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — Nehemiah 8:2 and 8:3, consecutive verses of the same assembly. Both of the Book of Mormon's audience-qualifications in this chapter answer them: 'you that can hear my words' here, and 'you little children, which can understand my words' at 2:40.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 6:10's ear-and-heart pairing ('hear with their ears, and understand with their heart') stands behind any English sentence of this shape, and Matthew 13:15 and Acts 28:27 quote it. But the mediation test is indecisive here — see the exclusion register at this verse — and Isaiah's clause is a judgment on people who will NOT hear, where Benjamin's is an invitation to people who will.
provenance.significance: Benjamin's opening does what Ezra's assembly does and states it as a condition of attendance: the audience is defined as those who can hear and understand, and the ears are the organ the text keeps naming. What the Book of Mormon adds is the third term — 'your minds that the mysteries of God may be unfolded to your view' — which converts a public reading of the law into an initiation. Nehemiah's people hear the law; Benjamin's are promised the mysteries.

2:9.note: 'Open your ears that ye may hear, and your hearts that ye may understand, and your minds that the mysteries of God may be unfolded to your view.' The ear-and-understanding pair, and the qualification of the audience by capacity to understand, are Nehemiah 8:2-3's, where both phrases are KJV singletons. 'Mysteries of God' is 1 Corinthians 4:1's singleton, already catalogued at Mosiah 1:3, so the sentence joins the Ezra assembly to the Pauline stewardship in one breath.

2:10.text: And saying, Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God, which made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are therein:

provenance.route: Acts 14:11-15 (with Acts 10:26) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “of like passions” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; James 5:17 has 'subject to like passions', which is the form the Book of Mormon's 'subject to all manner of infirmities' is closer to in construction. Acts 10:26's 'I myself also am a man' is the other KJV refusal of divine honour and has no shared wording.
provenance.significance: There are two scenes in the KJV where a crowd is about to treat a man as more than a man and he stops them: Cornelius falling at Peter's feet, and Lystra bringing oxen to Barnabas and Paul because 'the gods are come down to us in the likeness of men'. Both refusals take the same form Benjamin's does — do not fear me, I am what you are — and Acts 14:15 supplies the vocabulary of shared human nature. Benjamin then does what Paul does next in the same sentence: turns from himself to the God 'which made heaven, and earth', which is where Mosiah 2:20-25 goes.

2:10.note: 'I have not commanded you to come up hither, that ye should fear me, or that ye should think that I, of myself, am more than a mortal man; but I am like as yourselves, subject to all manner of infirmities in body and mind.' Little is reproduced verbally, but the move is one the KJV makes twice and only twice, and Acts 14:15's 'men of like passions with you' is its one fixed phrase. The link is filed here rather than at 2:11 because 2:10's refusal of fear is the half that matches Lystra; 2:26's 'I, even I, whom ye call your king, am no better than ye yourselves are' repeats it at the end of the speech.

2:11.text: And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength: this is the first commandment.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 6:5 via Mark 12:30 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The mediation is the finding and it needs stating carefully. tools/mediation-check.py reports one decisive point for Deuteronomy 6:5 — the Book of Mormon has 'might', which is Deuteronomy's word and not Mark's. That report is an artifact of how the diff aligns the two verses, because the Book of Mormon ALSO has 'mind' and 'strength', and neither is available from Deuteronomy 6:5 at all: the Hebrew shema in the KJV runs heart, soul, might, and 'mind' enters the English scriptures only in the Synoptic quotations. “with all thy mind” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, and all three are Synoptic quotations of the shema; Mark 12:30 is the one that has mind before strength, which is the Book of Mormon's order, since Luke 10:27 reverses them and Matthew 22:37 omits strength altogether.
provenance.significance: 'Might, mind, and strength' is not a biblical triad. It is the Deuteronomic term plus the two the New Testament added, with the Deuteronomic 'heart' and 'soul' dropped — a conflation that could only be made by someone holding both forms of the shema at once. Benjamin is not quoting the love-command either: he applies its measure to service rather than to love, 'to serve thee with all the might, mind, and strength which the Lord hath granted unto me', which is the move the whole speech makes from 2:17 onward — service of others as service of God.

2:11.note: 'To serve thee with all the might, mind, and strength which the Lord hath granted unto me.' Three of the shema's four measures, taken from two different KJV forms of it. Moderate rather than high because a triad of near-synonyms is easy to produce independently and because Benjamin's application is his own; but the presence of 'mind' rules out Deuteronomy 6:5 as the sole source, which is what makes this an OT-via-NT row rather than a Deuteronomic one. Note also 'kept and preserved by his matchless power', which repeats Mosiah 1:13's 'matchless and marvellous power' from the previous chapter.

2:12.text: I have coveted no man’s silver, or gold, or apparel.

provenance.other: “coveted no man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “with all humility of mind” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both in this speech. Nehemiah 5:14-18, the other biblical apologia by a ruler who did not live off the people, is a real rival for the taxes at 2:14 and is catalogued there; it has nothing corresponding to the blood at 2:27.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 2:12-29 is Paul's Miletus farewell, kept in Paul's order. Acts 20:18 'ye know, from the first day that I came into Asia, after what manner I have been with you at all seasons' → 2:12 'I have been suffered to spend my days in your service, even up to this time'. Acts 20:33 'I have coveted no man's silver, or gold' → 2:12 'have not sought gold nor silver'. Acts 20:34 'these hands have ministered unto my necessities' → 2:14 'I, myself, have labored with mine own hands'. Acts 20:26 'I am pure from the blood of all men' → 2:27 'that your blood should not come upon me'. Acts 20:25 'ye all … shall see my face no more' → 2:29 'I can no longer be your teacher, nor your king'. Five elements, one source-passage, and the same genre: a departing leader's self-defence before the people he has served, delivered because he is about to be taken from them.

2:12.note: 'I have not sought gold nor silver, nor no manner of riches of you.' The disclaimer is Paul's at Miletus, where 'coveted no man's silver, or gold' is a KJV singleton, and it is the first of five contacts with the same speech across the next eighteen verses. The rest are catalogued at 2:14, 2:27 and 2:28. What makes the passage rather than the phrase the source is that the Book of Mormon reproduces the sequence: service from the first day, no money taken, hands that laboured, innocence of blood, and a farewell.

2:13.text: Will ye steal, murder, and commit adultery, and swear falsely, and burn incense unto Baal, and walk after other gods whom ye know not;

provenance.other: “murder and commit adultery” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “steal murder” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — both Jeremiah 7:9, the only place in the KJV where the decalogue's prohibitions are strung as a rhetorical question. Hosea 4:2's list is 'swearing, and lying, and killing, and stealing, and committing adultery', with different verb forms; the Ten Commandments themselves are in the second person singular and negative.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 7 is the Temple Sermon: Jeremiah stands in the gate of the LORD's house and asks a people who have come to worship whether they mean to steal, murder and commit adultery and then stand in this house and say they are delivered. Benjamin is standing at his temple, addressing a people camped around it, and lists the same crimes — as things he has NOT suffered among them. The Book of Mormon has taken the temple-gate indictment and inverted it into a temple-gate acquittal.

2:13.note: 'Or that ye should murder, or plunder, or steal, or commit adultery.' The KJV strings these three verbs together once, at Jeremiah 7:9, and the Book of Mormon reorders them and adds 'plunder', which is in no KJV verse. Moderate rather than high because a list of capital crimes is the most predictable content such a sentence could have; what raises it above coincidence is the setting, since both lists are spoken at a temple to a congregation assembled for worship.

2:14.text: Yea, ye yourselves know, that these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with me.

provenance.other: “these hands have ministered” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “ye yourselves know” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — the same verse. The Book of Mormon has both halves: the labouring hands, and the appeal to the hearers as witnesses of it.
provenance.significance: Acts 20:34-35 gives the reason Paul worked: 'so labouring ye ought to support the weak'. Benjamin gives a different reason — that the people should not be laden with taxes — and the difference is the whole distance between an apostle and a king. But the sentence is built the same way and ends the same way, on the hearers' own testimony: 'ye yourselves know' becomes 'ye yourselves are witnesses this day', which also carries Acts 20:26's 'I take you to record this day'.

2:14.note: 'Even I, myself, have labored with mine own hands, that I might serve you … and of all these things which I have spoken, ye yourselves are witnesses this day.' Two KJV singletons from one verse of the Miletus speech, in the same relation to each other: the manual labour, and the audience called to confirm it. This is the second of the five contacts with Acts 20 catalogued in this chapter; see the argument at 2:12.

2:14.text: And he said, Woe unto you also, ye lawyers! for ye lade men with burdens grievous to be borne, and ye yourselves touch not the burdens with one of your fingers.

provenance.other: “grievous to be borne” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 23:4 and Luke 11:46, the same woe in two gospels. tools/mediation-check.py reports no decisive divergence between them at any point the Book of Mormon reproduces, so the choice has to be made by eye — and it is Luke's, on one word: Luke's lawyers 'lade men with burdens grievous to be borne', and the Book of Mormon has 'laden'. Matthew's Pharisees 'bind heavy burdens', a verb the Book of Mormon does not use.
provenance.alternative: Nehemiah 5:14-18, catalogued at this verse, accounts for the office and the taxes; Luke accounts for the wording. Neither displaces the other.
provenance.significance: The woe is against religious leaders who load a people with what they will not carry themselves, and its sting is in the second clause: 'ye yourselves touch not the burdens with one of your fingers.' Benjamin's answer to that clause is the whole of 2:14 — not only did he not lade them, he laboured with his own hands. He is stating, of a king, the exact opposite of what Jesus says of the lawyers, phrase for phrase, and the borrowed phrase is what makes the contrast legible.

2:14.note: 'That ye should not be laden with taxes, and that there should nothing come upon you which was grievous to be borne.' Both of the KJV verses containing this phrase are the same woe against leaders, and the Book of Mormon's 'laden' is Luke's verb rather than Matthew's. What Benjamin denies having done to his people is precisely what Luke 11:46 accuses the lawyers of doing to theirs, and the denial sits in the same sentence as the labouring hands of Acts 20:34 — so the verse is built out of two New Testament passages about leaders and their hands.

2:14.text: Now that which was prepared for me daily was one ox and six choice sheep; also fowls were prepared for me, and once in ten days store of all sorts of wine: yet for all this required not I the bread of the governor, because the bondage was heavy upon this people.

provenance.other: “the bread of the governor” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Nehemiah 5:14 and 5:18. No wording is reproduced by the Book of Mormon; the case is entirely one of matching content, which is why kjvSpecific is 'uncertain' here and 'yes' on the Acts 20 rows.
provenance.alternative: Acts 20:33-34, catalogued at 2:12 and 2:14, accounts for the not-taking and the labouring on its own and does so with reproduced wording. Nehemiah is proposed for what Acts does not have: the taxes.

2:14.note: 'That ye should not be laden with taxes, and that there should nothing come upon you which was grievous to be borne.' Paul at Miletus refused money and worked with his hands; he did not levy anything, because he governed nothing. The one biblical ruler who defends himself in these terms is Nehemiah, who for twelve years 'required not I the bread of the governor, because the bondage was heavy upon this people', and whose predecessors 'were chargeable unto the people'. Benjamin's sentence needs both sources, and this half is Nehemiah's — the same book, and within seven chapters, of the assembly that gave the chapter its staging at 2:7 and 2:9.

2:15.text: The like figure whereunto even baptism doth also now save us (not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God,) by the resurrection of Jesus Christ:

provenance.other: “the answer of a good conscience” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The KJV's other conscience formulas are different: Acts 24:16's 'a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men', 2 Timothy 1:3's 'pure conscience', Hebrews 13:18's 'a good conscience'. Only 1 Peter 3:21 puts 'answer' and 'conscience' and 'toward God' in one phrase, which is the phrase Benjamin has.
provenance.significance: In 1 Peter the answer of a good conscience toward God is what baptism IS — the thing the water enacts, in a passage about a covenant made in the presence of God. Benjamin uses the phrase twice in the chapter, at 2:15 and again at 2:27 ('walking with a clear conscience before God'), and the second time it is the ground on which he convenes the assembly that will end, four chapters later, in a covenant and a new name. The Book of Mormon has borrowed a baptismal formula for a covenant-renewal scene, which is what Mosiah 5-6 turns out to be.

2:15.note: 'That I can answer a clear conscience before God this day.' 'Answer' as a verb governing 'conscience' is not ordinary English and not ordinary KJV; the noun phrase behind it is 1 Peter 3:21's, a singleton. Moderate rather than high because the Book of Mormon converts the noun to a verb and substitutes 'clear' for 'good', so what is shared is a construction rather than a string. The clause is also the point where the Acts 20 farewell and this borrowing coincide: Paul is 'pure from the blood', Benjamin is clear in conscience, and both say 'this day'.

2:17.text: And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.

provenance.alternative: Ephesians 6:7 ('with good will doing service, as to the Lord, and not to men') and Colossians 3:23-24 say something adjacent in words closer to Benjamin's 'service', and neither has Matthew's identification of the served person with the judge.
provenance.significance: The identity Benjamin states — service of your fellow beings IS service of your God — is stated once in the KJV, by a king on a throne separating sheep from goats, and it is stated there as the criterion of judgement. Benjamin is a king, speaking about the service a king owes and is owed, and the sentence he arrives at is the sentence Matthew's King speaks. Note also what Matthew 25:46 supplies two verses later and this chapter takes at 2:33: 'everlasting punishment', a KJV singleton. The judgement scene is being drawn on at both ends of the sermon.

2:17.note: 'When ye are in the service of your fellow beings, ye are only in the service of your God.' Nothing verbal is reproduced, which is why this is filed as figural; the argument is that the KJV makes this equation exactly once and makes it in a king's mouth. What Benjamin does with it is characteristic — Matthew's King identifies himself with the served, and Benjamin instead makes the service transitive, so that the debt he has just refused to claim (2:15-16) is redirected to God at 2:19-24.

2:21.text: For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.

provenance.other: “live and move” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Acts 17:25 supplies the other half of Benjamin's clause: God 'giveth to all life, and breath, and all things' — the breath, the life, and the not-needing-anything that Mosiah 2:21 turns into 'lending you breath, that ye may live and move'.
provenance.significance: Paul at Athens is arguing that God needs nothing from his worshippers, which is precisely Benjamin's argument in 2:20-25: you cannot put God in your debt, because the breath you would thank him with is on loan. Two verses of the Areopagus speech supply both terms, and a third supplies this chapter's 2:37 ('dwelleth not in temples made with hands'). The Book of Mormon has read Acts 17:24-28 as a unit and distributed it across a sermon about indebtedness — including the sting Paul's Greek audience would have felt and Benjamin's does too: the giver of breath is not housed in the building you are camped around.

2:21.note: 'Him who hath created you from the beginning, and art preserving you from day to day, by lending you breath, that ye may live and move.' The KJV says 'live, and move' once. Benjamin's addition is the metaphor of a loan, which converts Paul's ontological claim into an accounting one and sets up the ledger of 2:23-24 — created, granted, blessed, paid, and still indebted. The 1830 'art preserving' (for 'is preserving') is one of the first edition's ungrammatical readings that later editions smoothed; it does not bear on the source.

2:21.text: So likewise ye, when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do.

provenance.other: “unprofitable servants” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Matthew 25:30 has the singular 'unprofitable servant', of a man who buried his talent — a different case, since Luke's servants have done everything they were told.
provenance.significance: Luke 17:7-10 is a small parable with two moves, and Benjamin makes both. First, Luke 17:9: 'Doth he thank that servant because he did the things that were commanded him? I trow not' — which is Mosiah 2:19-24's question about thanks and merit. Second, Luke 17:10: even after doing all that is commanded, the servant is unprofitable. Benjamin's version is harder than Luke's, because he inserts an infinite regress the parable does not have — God pays immediately, so obedience never closes the account and the debt grows: 'ye are still indebted unto him; and are, and will be, forever and ever'. The borrowed phrase is Luke's; the arithmetic is the Book of Mormon's.

2:21.note: 'If ye should serve him with all your whole soul, and yet ye would be unprofitable servants.' A KJV singleton reproduced with its logic intact — the conditional 'if ye should serve … and yet' is Luke 17:10's 'when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you' turned into a hypothetical. Below Skousen's threshold and not among his quotations; catalogued as a quotation under CONVENTIONS §2 because the clause and its argument are reproduced from an identifiable verse. Verse 24's 'of what have ye to boast?' completes Luke 17:9's question about thanks.

2:25.text: In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.

provenance.route: Genesis 2:7 and 3:19 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'The dust of the earth' occurs in nine KJV verses and cannot identify a source on its own; Genesis 2:7's formation is 'of the dust of the ground'. The reason for naming Genesis 3:19 rather than any of the nine is the return — Benjamin is 'about to yield up this mortal frame to its mother earth', which is 'unto dust shalt thou return' and nothing else.
provenance.significance: Benjamin's argument is a strange one and the strangeness is the point: you cannot say you are even as much as the dust, though you were made of it, because the dust belongs to its maker and you do not have even that standing. Genesis gives him both ends of the sentence — made of dust, returning to dust — and Abraham at Genesis 18:27 gives him its posture, 'I who am but dust and ashes', spoken while bargaining with God. Benjamin removes the bargaining position: Abraham's dust could still plead, and Benjamin's cannot claim.

2:25.note: 'Ye cannot say that thou art even as much as the dust of the earth; yet thou wast created of the dust of the earth: but behold, it belongeth to him who created you.' Filed as conceptual with kjvSpecific 'no' because every phrase here is common to all English Bibles; what makes it a link rather than an ambient biblicism is the pairing with 2:26, where the same speaker says 'I am also of the dust' and names his death as a yielding up to the earth, which completes Genesis 3:19's sentence in the order Genesis has it.

2:27.text: Wherefore I take you to record this day, that I am pure from the blood of all men.

provenance.route: Acts 20:26 (with Ezekiel 33:6) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “pure from the blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The idea is Ezekiel's watchman — if the watchman does not blow the trumpet, the blood of the slain 'will I require at the watchman's hand' (Ezekiel 33:6) — and Paul is applying Ezekiel to himself at Miletus. The Book of Mormon has Paul's application rather than Ezekiel's oracle: the leader declares himself clear, which Ezekiel never does.
provenance.significance: Benjamin gives two reasons for convening the assembly, and both are the reasons a departing teacher gives: 'that I might be found blameless, and that your blood should not come upon me, when I shall stand to be judged of God'. The clause 'this day' at 2:14, the innocence of blood here, and the farewell at 2:29 are Acts 20:26, 20:34 and 20:25 in the source's own order. What Benjamin adds to Paul is the judgement scene — the reckoning is not merely declared, it is dated to a future court.

2:27.note: 'That I might be found blameless, and that your blood should not come upon me, when I shall stand to be judged of God.' The formula is Paul's at Miletus, where it is a KJV singleton, and behind Paul stands Ezekiel's watchman. This is the fourth of the five Acts 20 contacts in this chapter; the fifth is the farewell at 2:29, and 2:28's 'rid my garments of your blood' takes the same idea to a different verse of Acts, catalogued there.

2:28.text: And when they opposed themselves, and blasphemed, he shook his raiment, and said unto them, Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean; from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles.

provenance.other: “shook his raiment” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Nehemiah 5:13 shakes a lap and Acts 13:51 shakes dust from feet; only Acts 18:6 shakes a garment and pairs the gesture with blood on the hearers' heads and the speaker's own cleanness.
provenance.significance: Benjamin's phrase is unintelligible without Acts 18:6 and immediately clear with it. 'Rid my garments of your blood' is not a figure the Old Testament uses — blood is on heads, or required at hands — and the only place in the KJV where a garment is shaken to disclaim responsibility for a people's blood is Paul at Corinth. That the Book of Mormon has both halves of the Pauline blood-idiom in consecutive verses (Acts 20:26's purity at 2:27, Acts 18:6's shaken garment at 2:28) is the kind of double contact that makes a single one credible.

2:28.note: 'That I might rid my garments of your blood, at this period of time when I am about to go down to my grave, that I might go down in peace.' The garment-and-blood gesture is Acts 18:6's, a KJV singleton, and it arrives one verse after Acts 20:26's 'pure from the blood'. The Book of Mormon has made a gesture of rejection into a gesture of discharge — Paul shakes his raiment at people who have refused him, Benjamin at people who have obeyed him.

2:28.text: Do therefore according to thy wisdom, and let not his hoar head go down to the grave in peace.

provenance.other: “to the grave in peace” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 2 Kings 22:20 has 'thou shalt be gathered into thy grave in peace', of Josiah, with 'gathered into' rather than 'go down to'; Genesis 42:38 and 44:29 bring gray hairs 'with sorrow to the grave' and lack the peace.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's quiet return to 1 Kings 2. Mosiah 1:9 took David's 'I go the way of all the earth' from 1 Kings 2:2; four verses later in the same charge, David tells Solomon not to let Joab's hoar head go down to the grave in peace, and it is that phrase — negated in the source, affirmed here — that Benjamin uses of his own death. Read together, Benjamin has taken David's deathbed speech and kept for himself the peace David denied his enemy. The Book of Mormon has quarried one chapter of 1 Kings twice in two chapters of Mosiah.

2:28.note: 'At this period of time when I am about to go down to my grave, that I might go down in peace.' A KJV singleton, and its one occurrence is in David's charge to Solomon — the passage Mosiah 1:9 already used. Recorded as an echo rather than an allusion because the phrase is idiomatic enough to have been written without a source and because its sense in 1 Kings 2:6 is inverted; the argument for it is proximity in the source to a borrowing already established one chapter earlier.

2:33.text: For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord’s body.

provenance.other: “drinketh damnation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon's 'to his own soul' replaces Paul's 'to himself'; the verb and its object are otherwise Paul's exactly, and the metaphor of drinking a judgement has no other KJV home.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is about the Lord's Supper — a covenant meal taken unworthily, by a congregation that has assembled and not discerned what it is assembled for. Benjamin is presiding over an assembly that is about to become a covenant (Mosiah 5), his people are camped around the temple with their sacrifices already offered (2:3), and the warning he issues to anyone who listeth to obey the evil spirit is the warning Paul issues to the unworthy communicant. The metalepsis is exact: the danger of an assembly is that some of those present will drink their own damnation at it.

2:33.note: 'The same drinketh damnation to his own soul.' A KJV singleton lifted whole, with the possessive changed. The verse then continues into two further borrowings — 'he receiveth for his wages an everlasting punishment', where 'wages' is Romans 6:23's figure and 'everlasting punishment' is Matthew 25:46's singleton, catalogued separately at this verse — so 2:33 carries three New Testament judgement formulas in one sentence.

2:33.text: And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal.

provenance.route: Matthew 25:46 (with Romans 6:23) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “everlasting punishment” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'The wages of' occurs in three, of which Romans 6:23 ('the wages of sin is death') is the only one that makes a punishment a wage. 'Die in your sins' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 8:24 twice over, which is the source of 'remaineth and dieth in his sins'.
provenance.significance: Matthew 25 is being used at both ends of this sermon: verse 40's identification of service with service of the King stands behind Mosiah 2:17, and verse 46's sentence stands here. The Book of Mormon fuses it with Romans 6:23, and the fusion changes the theology — Matthew's punishment is a destination one is sent to, Paul's death is a wage one has earned, and Benjamin's is both: 'he receiveth for his wages an everlasting punishment'. That is the same accounting metaphor the chapter has run since 2:23, now applied to the debtor who defaults.

2:33.note: 'For he receiveth for his wages an everlasting punishment, having transgressed the law of God, contrary to his own knowledge.' Three New Testament formulas meet in the verse — Paul's wage, Matthew's everlasting punishment, John 8:24's dying in one's sins — and each is a KJV singleton or near it. What the Book of Mormon supplies is the aggravation, 'contrary to his own knowledge', which none of the three has and which the whole chapter has been establishing since 2:34's claim that everyone present has been taught.

2:37.text: And said, O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?

provenance.other: “enemy of all righteousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon reads 'an enemy to all righteousness', with 'to' for 'of'; no other KJV verse contains the phrase in either preposition.
provenance.significance: Acts 13:10 is Paul's denunciation of Elymas the sorcerer, and the two charges it makes are the two Benjamin makes here: the man is a child of the devil, and he is the enemy of all righteousness. Benjamin's version supplies the mechanism Acts leaves implicit — 'he listeth to obey the evil spirit' — so that becoming the enemy of all righteousness is presented as a chosen allegiance rather than a character. That is the doctrine of the whole passage, from 2:32's warning about listing to obey to 2:33's 'contrary to his own knowledge'.

2:37.note: 'The same cometh out in open rebellion against God; therefore, he listeth to obey the evil spirit, and becometh an enemy to all righteousness.' A KJV singleton with one preposition changed, taken from the KJV's fiercest denunciation of a man in league with the devil. 'Open rebellion' is in no KJV verse and is the Book of Mormon's own; the borrowed phrase is what gives the sentence its scriptural force.

2:37.text: Howbeit the most High dwelleth not in temples made with hands; as saith the prophet,

provenance.route: Acts 7:48 / Acts 17:24 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “dwelleth not in temples made with hands” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 7:48 and Acts 17:24, and in both it is a New Testament speaker's gloss on Isaiah 66:1-2. The Old Testament itself never puts it this way; Isaiah asks 'where is the house that ye build unto me?', whose mediation was decided at 1 Nephi 17:39. Which of the two Acts verses is in view cannot be settled from the wording, since they are identical at every point the Book of Mormon reproduces.
provenance.significance: The sentence is doing something audacious in its setting. Benjamin is speaking from a tower at a temple, to a people camped in a ring around that temple with the doors of their tents turned toward it, and the doctrine he states is that the Lord does not dwell in unholy temples — with 'temple' meaning the man. Acts supplies the formula in both of its occurrences, and 1 Corinthians 3:16-17 supplies the transfer to the person ('ye are the temple of God'; 'if any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy'), which is the sense Benjamin has. The Areopagus verse is also the one that gave 2:21 its breath and motion, so the chapter takes both halves of Acts 17:24-28.

2:37.note: 'Therefore, the Lord hath no place in him, for he dwelleth not in unholy temples.' The KJV's phrase appears twice, both times in Acts, and the Book of Mormon compresses it — 'unholy temples' for 'temples made with hands' — which shifts the object from a building to a person and requires 1 Corinthians 3:16-17 to complete the thought. Moderate because the compression leaves only three words in common; the case is that the sentence cannot be assembled from the Old Testament, where this doctrine exists as a rhetorical question and not as a proposition.

2:38.text: And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name.

provenance.other: “ascendeth up for ever and ever” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Revelation 19:3 has 'her smoke rose up for ever and ever', in the past tense and of Babylon; only 14:11 has the present participle-form the Book of Mormon uses, and only 14:11 attaches it to torment rather than to a burning city.
provenance.significance: Revelation 14:11-12 is used as a unit across four verses of this chapter, in the source's order. Verse 11's ascending torment is Mosiah 2:38's 'flames ascendeth up forever and ever'; verse 12's 'here are they that keep the commandments of God' is Mosiah 2:41's 'those that keep the commandments of God'. Revelation places the endurance of the saints immediately after the smoke of the damned as a deliberate contrast, and Benjamin's peroration does the same thing at the same interval: the awful situation of the fallen at 2:40, the blessed and happy state of the obedient at 2:41.

2:38.note: 'Which is like an unquenchable fire, whose flames ascendeth up forever and ever.' A KJV singleton, with the 1830's uninflected 'ascendeth' after a plural subject preserving the source's verb form more exactly than the corrected text does. Note that the same verse of Revelation is cross-referenced by Hardy at Mosiah 3:27, one chapter later; the borrowing catalogued here is a separate and earlier occurrence of it.

2:38.text: Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.

provenance.other: “unquenchable fire” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; Luke 3:17 renders the same saying of John the Baptist as 'fire unquenchable', in the other word order, and Mark 9:43-48 has 'the fire that never shall be quenched'. The Book of Mormon has Matthew's order.
provenance.significance: John the Baptist's fire is a threshing image — the chaff separated from the wheat and burned — and it is about a judgement that is coming, not one already in progress. Benjamin uses the phrase for something internal and present: guilt and pain and anguish in the breast of a man who has not repented, 'which is like an unquenchable fire'. The simile is the Book of Mormon's own move; what it borrows is the adjective, and the adjective in the KJV belongs to one verse.

2:38.note: 'Doth fill his breast with guilt, and pain, and anguish, which is like an unquenchable fire.' Moderate rather than high: a single compound adjective is thin evidence, and Mark and Luke both say something close in different words. It is filed as a link rather than passed over because the Book of Mormon has Matthew's exact form, and because the second half of the same clause takes another judgement singleton from Revelation 14:11.

2:41.text: Here is the patience of the saints: here are they that keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus.

provenance.other: “keep the commandments of God” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 12:17 and Revelation 14:12 — the phrase the Book of Mormon uses constantly belongs, in this exact form, to the Apocalypse. Revelation 14:12 is the one that stands next to a description of endless torment.
provenance.significance: The pairing is the argument. Mosiah 2:38-41 sets the never-ending torment of the unrepentant against the never-ending happiness of those who keep the commandments and 'hold out faithful to the end', and it does so in four verses; Revelation 14:11-12 sets the smoke that ascends for ever against the patience of the saints who keep the commandments of God, and it does so in two. Both make endurance the answer to endlessness, and both use the same two phrases to do it. Benjamin's 'hold out faithful to the end' is what Revelation calls the patience of the saints.

2:41.note: 'Those that keep the commandments of God … and if they hold out faithful to the end, they are received into Heaven, that thereby they may dwell with God, in a state of never ending happiness.' The phrase is one of two KJV occurrences, and the other, Revelation 12:17, is in a war passage with nothing else in common. The case for 14:12 is its position: the Book of Mormon reproduces Revelation's own sequence, torment then endurance, across the same short span. Moderate because 'keep the commandments of God' had by Mosiah long since become the Book of Mormon's own idiom.
